comments.author: @sciolio1
comments.text: Something to think about. If responsibility for accidents is pushed up to the manufacturer or the server farm that is running the car's brain, then those companies are on the hook for infinite and indefinite liability, for all the cars they operate, and personally owned cars with no self driving will see the cost of private insurance policies becoming too high to afford. However, if we keep the responsibility at the owner of the car, regardless if they are "driving" the vehicle, then it won't affect the insurance industry in the slightest, and liability policies for privately owned vehicles will still be affordable. Insurance companies can lobby, I can't see how this goes any other way.

comments.author: @evan421
comments.text:
Tesla will easily be the leader in autonomy. There are three primary factors.  1) Cost - A Tesla is 1/10 the cost to operate vs a Waymo.  2) Scalability -  Tesla's vision plus neural nets approach is already proving it can scale much faster than Waymo.  In two months from launch, Tesla now covers a larger area of California than Waymo (operating for over a decade).  3). Data advantage -  Tesla already has well over a billion miles of driving data.  The scalability factor will only widen this advantage for Tesla.   

The thing many people miss is that autonomy's total addressable market is not just ride-share (~3%), it is transportation and the car ownership model (~$10 trillion).

comments.author: @listerdave1240
comments.text:
@7:00 I don't see why the responsibility should be an issue, in my opinion it does not change. Today if you're driving and crash a determination is made as to who or what is responsible. If the crash was caused by a defect in the car's design or manufacture then the manufacturer is responsible. I don't see why it would be any different for an autonomous car. The only difference is that the defect in the car is in a part that didn't exist before, the autonomous driving system.   I don't see why a failure in that should be treated differently from, say, a failure in the steering mechanism causing a manually driven car to crash.
Same would apply for autonomous planes, and in fact already does today. When a partly autonomous function of the 737MAX malfunctioned the responsibility was placed squarely on the manufacturer.
